strengths: Provides a novel and conceptually clean reformulation of data-value-based selection as a deterministic MDP / sequential decision-making problem, with a well-defined objective (Eq. 1) that operationalizes the informal notion of 'good selection curves' used implicitly in prior evaluation protocols.

The reinterpretation of existing semi-value methods (Data Shapley, Beta Shapley, Data Banzhaf) as myopic ADP solutions with linear reward surrogates (Theorem 4.1, Appendix C) is an elegant theoretical unification that offers plausible explanatory power for known empirical phenomena (e.g., why Data Shapley works well on heterogeneous data).

The curvature-based (1-c)^2 approximation guarantee (Theorem 4.6) is a nontrivial extension connecting submodularity/curvature to sequential (multi-budget) selection performance, and is empirically validated with a controlled synthetic curvature experiment (Section 7.2, Appendix I) that shows the predicted qualitative degradation trend.

The bipartite coverage-based surrogate is a reasonable, more expressive alternative to linear surrogate utility models, and the authors provide supporting theoretical claims (monotonicity/submodularity preservation, greedy optimality under correct specification).
Experiments span eight diverse OpenML datasets against nine baselines with results averaged over 20 runs, providing reasonably broad (if small-scale) empirical coverage.
weaknesses: The 'optimal' DynamicProgramming baseline requires evaluating the ground-truth utility (via actual model retraining) for exponentially many subsets, and RQ1 experiments are therefore restricted to toy-scale settings (20 training points). This severely limits the practical relevance and generalizability of the reported 'performance gaps,' and it is somewhat unsurprising/near-circular that a method with oracle access to the exact evaluation metric being plotted outperforms methods that do not have this access.

Table 1 contains an apparent inconsistency: the 'Average' and 'Std Dev' rows (0.255, 0.043, etc.) do not match a simple average of the per-dataset accuracies shown above them (which are all in the 0.6-0.9 range), suggesting an error in the table or unclear/undocumented computation, which undermines confidence in the quantitative results.

The theoretical guarantee for the bipartite approximation (Theorem G.3) is conditioned on the surrogate utility being 'correctly specified and learned,' which is a strong and largely unverifiable assumption in practice; no theoretical or empirical characterization of the approximation error when this condition fails is provided.

The claimed computational efficiency of the bipartite method is not clearly substantiated: Algorithm 2 requires sampling K random subsets and evaluating their accuracy to calibrate the similarity threshold, which itself requires model retraining, but the paper does not quantify or compare this cost against standard Shapley-style Monte Carlo estimation.

Experimental scale is uniformly small (50-100 training points, with only 500-1000 test points and budgets capped at 20-100 selected samples), raising concerns about whether the demonstrated advantages of the proposed method generalize to realistic dataset sizes and more complex models than logistic regression.

The equivalence claimed in Theorem 4.1/Lemma C.1 between game-theoretic values and the linear-surrogate ADP solution is only asymptotic (as number of samples N→∞) and relies on a different weighting formulation (weighted least squares) than the original marginal-contribution-averaging definition in Section 2.2, so the practical tightness of this 'equivalence' for finite-sample estimators actually used in experiments is not clearly established.

No statistical significance testing accompanies the reported mean ± std results, and qualitative claims in Section 7.3 (e.g., specific sample counts needed to reach given accuracy) are read directly off figures without formal statistical support.

The related-work differentiation from Wang et al. (2024a) is with a conference tutorial rather than a peer-reviewed paper, which is an unusual and somewhat weak comparison point for establishing novelty; the more substantive related empirical work (Wang et al., 2024b) is only briefly discussed.

strengths: The paper proposes a conceptually clean unifying lens: casting data selection via value-ranking as a sequential decision problem solvable exactly by dynamic programming, and reinterpreting Data Shapley/Beta Shapley/Data Banzhaf as myopic ADP solutions with a linear surrogate reward.

The curvature-based (1-c)^2 approximation-ratio result (Theorem 4.6) for semi-value rankings under monotone submodular utilities is a reasonable theoretical contribution and gives an interpretable explanation for why Data Shapley degrades on datasets with high data substitutability, aligning with prior empirical observations (Wang et al., 2024b).

The bipartite/coverage-based surrogate utility idea is intuitive and the paper attempts to establish that greedy selection on this surrogate preserves monotonicity/submodularity (Appendix G), which is a sensible design choice for scalability relative to exact DP.

The experimental protocol (selection curves, multiple OpenML datasets, averaging over 20 runs) follows established data-valuation evaluation conventions, making the setup easy to relate to prior literature.
weaknesses: The central 'optimal' baseline (DynamicProgramming) requires evaluating the ground-truth utility U(S) for essentially all subsets (or at least performing full backward induction), which needs actual model retraining for exponentially many subsets. This is only feasible because experiments are run on extremely small samples (20 training points for RQ1, 50-100 for RQ3) — far from the LLM/foundation-model data-selection setting invoked in the introduction. The 'significant performance gap' finding in RQ1 is therefore not surprising: it merely shows that an intractable oracle beats practical heuristics, and provides limited actionable insight since the oracle cannot scale.

The core practical contribution (bipartite surrogate) is a fairly simple heuristic — thresholded feature-distance edges gated by label match between train and validation points (Algorithm 2), essentially a tuned k-NN coverage score. No approximation bound is given for how well this surrogate approximates the true utility function; Theorem G.2/G.3 only show the surrogate itself is monotone submodular and that greedy is optimal *for that surrogate*, which is a fairly weak and somewhat circular guarantee — it says nothing about closeness to the ground-truth utility, undermining the claim that this 'preserves theoretical guarantees' for the actual selection problem.

Table 1 contains numbers that are internally inconsistent: the reported 'Average' and 'Std Dev' rows (e.g., 0.255, 0.043, 0.251...) do not match the per-dataset entries above them (which are mostly in the 0.6–0.9 range). This is a clear correctness/quality-control problem that raises doubts about the reliability of the reported quantitative results throughout the paper.

All experiments use only Logistic Regression as the trained model on small tabular/embedding datasets; there is no validation on deep networks or more realistic large-scale settings, despite the introduction motivating the work with LLM fine-tuning and modern deep learning data curation (citing Schoch et al., 2023 and Wang et al., 2024a/b). This significantly limits the demonstrated significance and generality of the proposed framework.

Several of the theoretical contributions largely restate or lightly repackage known facts: the equivalence between semi-value weighted-marginal-contribution formulas and a 'linear reward + myopic policy' ADP interpretation (Theorem 4.1) is essentially a relabeling of the well-known linear/modular structure of Shapley-type value; the reduction of ranking-induced greedy selection to submodular curvature guarantees closely follows prior curvature-based submodular approximation results (e.g., Balkanski et al., 2016, explicitly credited as inspiration) rather than introducing fundamentally new machinery.

RQ2's curvature experiment relies on a synthetic message-passing feature-averaging scheme within a toy 3-class classification problem to 'induce' curvature; it is unclear this construction faithfully represents real curvature regimes encountered in practical datasets, limiting the external validity of the empirical validation of Theorem 4.6.

No wall-clock/computational cost comparison is provided between the bipartite method, the exact DP oracle, and baseline valuation methods, despite efficiency being a central selling point of the proposed approximation scheme.

The claim of establishing 'the first systematic framework that unifies data values for sequential data' is an overreach given that connections between Shapley/Banzhaf values, submodularity, and greedy/dynamic-programming style selection are well-trodden ground in cooperative game theory and submodular optimization literature.

strengths: The paper offers a genuinely unifying theoretical lens: framing data valuation for selection as a deterministic MDP solvable by dynamic programming, and showing that Data Shapley, Beta Shapley, and Data Banzhaf can all be recovered as myopic reward-function approximations (linear surrogate + greedy policy) within this ADP framework (Theorem 4.1, Appendix C). This is a novel and clarifying reinterpretation of existing valuation methods.

The curvature-based analysis (Theorem 4.6) gives a principled, quantitative explanation for a previously only empirically observed phenomenon (semi-value methods degrade on datasets with high data substitutability), and the paper explicitly links this to prior empirical findings (Wang et al., 2024b), strengthening its explanatory value.

The paper is thorough in its proofs: linear utility optimality (Theorem 4.3/Appendix D), submodular approximation guarantees (Appendix E), and the bipartite coverage surrogate's preservation of monotonicity/submodularity and greedy optimality (Appendix G) are all worked out in detail rather than merely asserted.

The experimental section is reasonably comprehensive: it benchmarks against nine baselines on eight diverse OpenML datasets, includes a dedicated dynamic-programming oracle to empirically quantify the optimality gap of existing methods (RQ1), and a controlled synthetic experiment (message-passing curvature manipulation) that directly validates the theoretical curvature prediction (RQ2), which is a nice touch connecting theory to controlled empirical evidence.

The proposed bipartite surrogate method shows consistent, sometimes substantial, improvements over strong baselines across all eight datasets (Table 1, Figure 4), particularly in early-selection-stage efficiency, which is the stated practical goal.
weaknesses: The exact DP oracle used as a comparison baseline is only tractable for training sets of size 20 (Appendix H.5), which is far from realistic data-selection scenarios (e.g., LLM fine-tuning data curation, mentioned as motivation in the intro). This limits how much the 'gap to optimality' results in RQ1 generalize to practically relevant dataset scales.

The link between the theoretical DP/ADP framework and the practical bipartite algorithm is somewhat loose: Theorem G.3's optimality guarantee requires the bipartite surrogate to be 'correctly learned,' but Algorithm 2's threshold-selection procedure is heuristic (based on empirical coverage-vs-accuracy correlation on sampled subsets) with no guarantee of recovering the true utility structure, so the practical relevance of the optimality theorem is unclear.

The curvature approximation bound (1-c)^2 is not benchmarked against tighter, well-established bounds from the classical submodular-curvature literature (e.g., Conforti–Cornuejols-style (1-e^{-c})/c bounds), so it's unclear whether this is a genuinely tighter/novel guarantee or a looser restatement of known results applied to the sequential-selection setting.

Section 6 (value functions vs. reward functions) introduces an interesting alternative value definition (v*(i) = n - t*(i)) but it is not empirically evaluated or connected back to the bipartite method, making it feel like an underdeveloped side note rather than an integrated contribution.

The sequential-selection objective (uniform average of U(S_k) across all budgets, Eq. 1) is adopted without strong justification or comparison to alternative weightings (e.g., practitioners may care more about specific budget regimes); no sensitivity analysis is provided for this design choice.

Experiments are restricted to small tabular/text/image datasets with a simple logistic regression target model and small train/validation/test splits (e.g., 50-100 training points), which is a narrow testbed given the paper's motivating claims about large-scale data curation for foundation models.

No statistical significance testing is reported alongside the mean/standard-deviation comparisons in Table 1, and the RQ2 curvature experiment description in the appendix is fairly brief relative to the strength of the claims made about it in the main text.

strengths: Provides a novel and coherent theoretical framework that reformulates data selection as a finite-horizon deterministic MDP with an exact DP solution, and rigorously shows that existing semi-value methods (Shapley, Banzhaf, Beta Shapley) can be derived as regression coefficients that induce myopic linear-surrogate policies in this ADP view (Theorems 4.1–4.4, with detailed proofs in the appendix). This gives a principled explanation for known empirical phenomena (e.g., why Data Shapley struggles on redundant/heterogeneous data).

The curvature-based approximation bound (1-c)^2 for semi-value rankings under submodular utilities is a clean, interpretable theoretical contribution that unifies prior curvature-based sample-complexity results from the OPS literature.

The proposed bipartite coverage surrogate is simple, scalable, and comes with an explicit (though conditional) end-to-end approximation guarantee, and is empirically shown to have substantially lower utility-approximation error than linear/game-theoretic/MLP surrogates (Table 3).

Experimental validation is unusually extensive: eight OpenML datasets with detailed selection curves, a dedicated exact-DP optimality gap study (RQ1), a controlled curvature/substitutability ablation (RQ2), large-budget (500-point) evaluation, and a large-scale LLM instruction-selection experiment on DATE-LM with Llama-3.1-8B, including multiple embedding backends and computational cost analysis.

The paper is transparent about the limitations of its own theoretical guarantees (e.g., Remark H.3 explicitly notes the sandwich conditions may not hold in practice, and RQ2 explicitly states substitutability is only a qualitative curvature proxy), which strengthens the credibility of the claims.
weaknesses: The core theoretical guarantee for the proposed bipartite method (Theorem H.2) depends on idealized 'sandwich' conditions that the authors themselves acknowledge frequently fail to hold for the actual coverage surrogate used in experiments; the practical claim is thus weaker than a formal end-to-end guarantee and rests mainly on empirical MSE comparisons.

The RQ2 curvature experiments use within-class feature-averaging 'substitutability' as only a qualitative, indirect proxy for curvature c, and the true curvature of the constructed utility is never computed, so the connection to Theorem 4.4's quantitative (1-c)^2 bound is suggestive rather than a direct empirical validation.

The exact DP optimality baseline (RQ1) is only feasible for very small datasets (20 training points, 1000 retraining steps), limiting the generality of the reported 8-24% performance gaps to a narrow regime; it is unclear how this gap behaves at realistic dataset sizes where DP is intractable.

Most classical experiments rely on a single target model (logistic regression), and the bipartite coverage utility itself is a fairly coarse binary-threshold construct that may not transfer straightforwardly to more complex model classes or non-metric feature spaces.

The LLM-scale (DATE-LM) improvements over strong baselines (RDS+, Random) are modest (roughly 1 percentage point on average) and partially rely on a similarity-based fallback once coverage saturates early (after only 1-5 selections in some tasks), which somewhat undercuts the 'coverage-driven' narrative for the bulk of the 10k-example budget.

Some terminology choices (e.g., calling the surrogate+myopic-policy approach 'approximate dynamic programming') are acknowledged by the authors to diverge from standard ADP usage, which could cause confusion despite the clarifying remark.

The definition of optimal data values as v*(i) = n - t*(i) (Section 6) is a relatively thin theoretical contribution that mostly restates the DP-derived ordering without offering new algorithmic or estimation insight beyond what Section 3.2 already establishes.

strengths: The paper offers a conceptually appealing unifying lens: casting data selection as a finite-horizon deterministic MDP and showing that Shapley/Banzhaf/Beta-Shapley rankings arise as myopic greedy policies under specific linear-surrogate regression characterizations (Theorem 4.1, with detailed proofs in Appendices B-F).

The curvature-based approximation guarantee (Theorem 4.4, (1-c)^2 bound) gives a principled, falsifiable explanation for when/why semi-value rankings fail, and is reasonably well supported by a controlled message-passing substitutability experiment (Section 7.2/Appendix K).

The bipartite coverage surrogate is simple, provably submodular, and empirically shows consistent gains across eight OpenML datasets and in a large-scale LLM instruction-selection setting (DATE-LM/Llama-3.1-8B), with reasonably thorough appendices (complexity analysis, embedding ablations, computational cost).
Extensive and transparent appendix material, including proofs, related-work positioning against concurrent work (e.g., GraphFilter), and detailed experimental protocols aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The connection between the elaborate DP/ADP theory (Sections 3-4) and the actual proposed method (bipartite coverage + greedy, Section 5) is loose: the practical algorithm is a fairly standard max-coverage/set-cover heuristic that does not obviously follow from or require the sequential-decision framing, and the paper itself concedes the 'sandwich conditions' needed to connect the two do not hold in practice, reducing Theorem H.2 to a non-binding idealization while the real justification is purely empirical (Table 3).

The central 'optimality gap' claim (RQ1, Table 1) is established only on toy-scale settings (20 training points, logistic regression, 100 validation points); it is unclear whether the reported 8-24% gaps to exact DP generalize to realistic dataset sizes or model classes, since exact DP is exponential and was never tested beyond these small instances.

Some reported numbers raise soundness concerns: Table 3 shows MSE values of 2.29-2.40 for BetaShap/DataShap surrogates evaluating a utility that should be a bounded accuracy-like quantity, which is difficult to reconcile without further explanation and suggests a possible artifact of the 'intercept-only refit' procedure used for fairness, rather than a genuine indictment of linear surrogates.

The 'unification' explicitly excludes LOO (acknowledged in Remark D.3) and only covers semi-values in specific parameter ranges (a,b>1 for Beta Shapley), so the claimed generality of the ADP reinterpretation is narrower than the abstract/intro suggest.

Curvature is never directly measured in the experiments; 'substitutability' via feature averaging is used only as a qualitative proxy, so the quantitative validation of the (1-c)^2 bound is indirect and largely illustrative rather than a rigorous test of the theorem.

In the large-budget (500) and LLM fine-tuning experiments, the proposed method's advantage is often marginal or tied with baselines (many ties in Table 2; ~1% gain over RDS+ in Table 6 with overlapping standard deviations), weakening the practical significance claims relative to the strong framing in the abstract.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with any ethical or societal considerations specific to data selection/valuation (e.g., fairness in whose data gets excluded).

strengths: Novel and coherent theoretical framework casting data selection as a finite-horizon deterministic MDP solved via dynamic programming, with a rigorous, well-proven characterization of existing semi-value methods (Shapley, Banzhaf, Beta Shapley) as myopic linear-surrogate approximations (Theorems 4.1-4.2, with full proofs in Appendices B-F).

The curvature-based approximation bound (1-c)^2 (Theorem 4.4) gives a principled, quantitative explanation for when and why game-theoretic data values fail for selection, unifying prior empirical observations about Data Shapley's behavior on heterogeneous vs. redundant data.

The proposed bipartite coverage surrogate is simple, cheap to compute, provably submodular (Proposition 5.2), and comes with an end-to-end (1-ε)(1-1/e) guarantee under stated sandwich conditions (Theorem H.2), while the paper is candid that these conditions are idealized and may not hold exactly in practice (Remark H.3) — an honest treatment of limitations.

Extensive empirical validation: (1) direct comparison to exact DP on small-scale problems quantifying the optimality gap of existing methods, (2) a controlled curvature/substitutability ablation supporting the theoretical degradation prediction, (3) eight OpenML benchmarks showing consistent improvements from the bipartite method, and (4) a large-scale LLM instruction-selection experiment on the DATE-LM benchmark with LoRA fine-tuning of Llama-3.1-8B, showing the framework's practical relevance beyond toy settings.

High reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, dataset splits, baseline implementations (via OpenDataVal), computational complexity analysis, and multiple ablations (embedding backbones, seeds) are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The 'ADP' framing is somewhat stretched terminology-wise (self-acknowledged in Remark 3.2); the actual mechanism is 'linear/bipartite surrogate + myopic greedy policy,' which is a much narrower instantiation than the classical ADP literature (value function approximation, rollout, lookahead), so readers unfamiliar with this caveat could be misled by the framing in the abstract/intro.

The exact-DP optimality-gap experiments (RQ1) are necessarily restricted to very small training sets (20 points) due to exponential DP complexity, limiting how strongly the 'substantial performance gap' claim generalizes to realistic dataset sizes where practitioners actually apply data valuation.

RQ2's curvature analysis uses message-passing-induced 'substitutability' only as a qualitative proxy for curvature c; the true curvature is never computed, so the connection to the (1-c)^2 bound is illustrative/consistent rather than a tight quantitative validation of the theorem.

The LLM fine-tuning improvement (BipCov vs. RDS+, ~1 point average) is real but modest, and the reference-set construction inherits a label-leakage caveat from the DATE-LM benchmark design that is only briefly flagged; results across Table 6/7 use different seed protocols (multi-seed vs. single-seed) which slightly complicates direct comparison.

The 'optimal data values' proposal in Section 6 (v*(i) = n - t*(i) as a DP-sequence encoding) is conceptually interesting but underdeveloped — it is not empirically evaluated as a standalone contribution, and non-uniqueness/tie-breaking issues are only briefly acknowledged.
